title: Combinatorial pharmacogenomic test for successful antidepressant treatment of a major depressive disorder
abstract: Introduction. The combinatorial pharmacogenomic test has shown the potential to predict antidepressant response, tolerability, selection, and dosage in the treatment of a major depressive disorder. A case of successful management of antidepressant therapy adjustment is reported by using the combinatorial pharmacogenomic test. Case Report. A 53-year old man, severely disabled due to a rare genetic disease, Usher syndrome type 3, was treated with numerous antidepressants. However, episodes of major depression recurred, along with frequent suicidal thoughts. A combinatorial pharmacogenomic test was considered to design a potentially effective antidepressant therapy. Conclusion. According to the results of the combinatorial pharmacogenomic test, the patient constantly received inadequate antidepressant therapy, which did not lead to an improvement of depression due to moderate gene-drug interaction. The patient was prescribed nortriptyline, which proved to be one of the few most adequate according to the test. He showed improvement with subjectively more tolerable depression without suicidal thoughts and episodes of major depression. This case showed that the combinatorial pharmacogenomic testing may contribute to better selection of antidepressant therapy.
